results.title: GPU Prices 2026: H100 From $3.49/hr, RTX 5070 at +58%
results.author: Axis Intelligence Research
highlights:
> Prices verified on October 2, 2026. Every price on this page was read from the vendor’s live pricing page, public price API or retail listing on that date. AWS Capacity Block rates effective October 7, 2026 are taken from AWS’s own announcement on its pricing page.

Renting one NVIDIA H100 for an hour costs $3.49 on Runpod and $12.29 on Microsoft Azure — the same chip, listed on public pricing pages on October 2, 2026. Axis Intelligence Research’s GPU Hour Premium Ratio puts the hyperscaler list premium at 2.93x the neocloud median, and AWS is raising every GPU Capacity Block rate by roughly 15% on October 7.

...

How much does a GPU cost in October 2026? In the cloud, an NVIDIA H100 lists between $3.49 and $12.29 per GPU-hour on-demand; the neocloud median is $3.99. A B200 lists from $6.69 to $8.60. On the consumer side, the cheapest new RTX 5070 on Newegg was $869.99 against a $549 launch price — 58% above MSRP.

...

1. According to Axis Intelligence Research, hyperscalers list the NVIDIA H100 at 2.93 times the neocloud median price — $11.68 versus $3.99 per GPU-hour on-demand, as of October 2, 2026 (GPU Hour Premium Ratio, GHPR).
2. AWS raises EC2 Capacity Block GPU rates about 15% effective October 7, 2026, taking an H100 accelerator-hour from $5.191 to $5.970 and a B200 from $12.355 to $14.208, per AWS’s pricing page.
3. An 8-GPU H100 server rented on-demand for three years costs $2.58 million on Azure and $734,000 on Runpod, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s list-price TCO calculation.
4. The cheapest new GeForce RTX 5070 on Newegg cost $869.99 on October 2, 2026, 58% above the $549 price NVIDIA announced at CES in January 2025.
5. Azure’s spot price for an 8x H100 VM is 82% below its own on-demand rate — $18.17 versus $98.32 per hour in US East, per Microsoft’s Retail Prices API.

...

### H100 on-demand price per GPU-hour by provider (October 2, 2026)

| Provider | Instance / SKU | Listed price | GPUs | Price per GPU-hour | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Runpod | H100 SXM Pod (Secure Cloud) | $3.49/hr | 1 | $3.49 | Runpod pricing |

...

### What does AWS charge for an H100?

AWS’s per-accelerator figure that we verified is the EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML rate — a reservation you book for a fixed window, not open-ended on-demand. On October 2, 2026 the p5.48xlarge (8x H100) Capacity Block rate in US East (N. Virginia) was $41.528 per instance-hour, or $5.191 per H100. AWS’s pricing page states that from October 7, 2026, the P5 rate becomes $5.970 per accelerator across all available regions. Axis Intelligence Research did not verify a current AWS on-demand p5 rate for this snapshot, so AWS is excluded from the on-demand table rather than estimated.

## Why Is AWS Raising GPU Prices in October 2026?

AWS publishes the reason in one line: Capacity Block reservation prices are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand. The October 7, 2026 update moves every GPU family up by the same proportion.

### AWS EC2 Capacity Block rate change, effective October 7, 2026

| Instance family | GPU | Rate before (per accelerator-hour) | Rate from Oct 7, 2026 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | B300 | $14.040 | $16.146 | +15.0% |
| P6-B200 | B200 | $12.355 | $14.208 | +15.0% |
| P5en | H200 | $6.865 | $7.895 | +15.0% |
| P5e | H200 | $5.970 | $6.866 | +15.0% |
| P5 | H100 | $5.191 | $5.970 | +15.0% |
| P4de | A100 80GB | $2.214 | $2.546 | +15.0% |
| P4d | A100 40GB | $1.475 | $1.696 | +15.0% |

Source: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing, retrieved October 2, 2026. “Before” rates are the US East (N. Virginia) or US-region rates listed on the same page; percentage change is an Axis Intelligence Research calculation.

A uniform 15% move across seven GPU generations — including a 2020-era A100 40GB — tells you this is not a scarcity signal about one chip. Capacity Blocks are AWS’s mechanism for guaranteed short-term cluster access, and a flat repricing across the whole catalog reads as AWS re-pricing guaranteed availability itself. Buyers who only need interruptible capacity should read this as a reason to look at spot and neocloud rates, not as proof that GPUs in general got 15% more expensive.

## How Much Does a B200 or H200 Cost per Hour?

### Blackwell and H200 per-GPU-hour prices (October 2, 2026)

| GPU | Provider | Pricing model | Price per GPU-hour | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | Lambda | On-demand instance | $6.69 | Lambda pricing |
| B200 | Runpod | On-demand Pod | $6.79 | Runpod pricing |
| B200 | CoreWeave | On-demand, 8x HGX ($68.80/hr) | $8.60 | CoreWeave pricing |
| B200 | Lambda | 1-Click Cluster, 256+ GPUs, 2 weeks–1 year | $8.87 | Lambda pricing |
| B200 | Google Cloud | DWS Flex-start, a4-highgpu-8g ($64.44/hr) | $8.06 | Google Cloud pricing |
| B200 | AWS | Capacity Block, from Oct 7, 2026 | $14.21 | AWS pricing |
| B300 | Runpod | On-demand Pod | $7.89 | Runpod pricing |
| H200 | Runpod | On-demand Pod | $4.59 | Runpod pricing |
| H200 | CoreWeave | On-demand, 8x HGX ($50.44/hr) | $6.31 | CoreWeave pricing |
| H200 | Google Cloud | On-demand, a3-ultragpu-8g ($84.81/hr) | $10.60 | Google Cloud pricing |

One detail that most rate cards hide: Lambda’s B200 is cheaper on-demand ($6.69) than in its own 1-Click Clusters ($8.87–$9.86). The cluster price buys guaranteed multi-node capacity with interconnect, not a per-GPU discount. Google Cloud does not list an on-demand price for its A4 (B200) VM at all; the cheapest public path is DWS Flex-start at $64.44 per 8-GPU hour.

...

### Will AWS GPU prices go up in October 2026?

Yes, for Capacity Blocks. AWS’s pricing page states that from October 7, 2026, per-accelerator Capacity Block rates rise to $5.970 for P5 (H100), $14.208 for P6-B200 and $16.146 for P6-B300 — about 15% above prior rates. AWS states On-Demand and Savings Plans prices are unchanged.

results.title: AWS verteuert reservierte Nvidia-GPU-Kapazität
results.author: Tim Eichler
highlights:
- Tim Eichler 
- Oktober 3, 2026 

 Grzegorz Walczak

Amazon Web Services hebt die Preise für bestimmte reservierte GPU-Kapazitäten an. Vom 7. Oktober 2026 an gelten für mehrere mit Nvidia-Beschleunigern ausgestattete EC2-Instanzfamilien höhere Sätze bei den sogenannten Capacity Blocks for ML. Betroffen sind sowohl aktuelle Blackwell-Chips als auch ältere Nvidia-A100-GPUs. Andere Preismodelle von AWS werden durch die angekündigte Änderung dagegen nicht verteuert.

AWS Capacity Blocks ermöglichen Unternehmen, Rechenkapazität mit leistungsfähigen Beschleunigern für einen festgelegten Zeitraum im Voraus zu reservieren. Das Angebot richtet sich vor allem an rechenintensive Anwendungen wie das Training und die Anpassung von KI-Modellen. Die Preise richten sich nach AWS-Angaben nach Angebot und Nachfrage und werden regelmäßig angepasst.

## Rund 15 Prozent höhere Preise ab 7. Oktober

Für die Nvidia-basierten Instanzfamilien steigt das Preisniveau nach einem Vergleich der bisherigen und der ab 7. Oktober geltenden Sätze um rund 15 Prozent. AWS selbst veröffentlicht für den Stichtag konkrete neue Preise pro Beschleuniger und Stunde.

Am oberen Ende steht die P6-B300-Familie mit Nvidia-B300-Beschleunigern. Hier beträgt der neue Satz 16,146 Dollar je Accelerator-Stunde. Für die P6-B200-Familie mit B200-Chips werden 14,208 Dollar fällig. Bei Instanzen mit Nvidia H200 liegen die neuen Preise bei 7,895 Dollar für P5en und 6,866 Dollar für P5e. Für die mit H100-GPUs ausgestattete P5-Familie nennt AWS 5,970 Dollar je Beschleuniger und Stunde.

Auch ältere Generationen werden teurer. Für P4de mit Nvidia A100 und 80 Gigabyte Grafikspeicher steigt der maßgebliche Satz von zuvor 2,214 Dollar auf 2,546 Dollar je GPU-Stunde. Bei P4d mit A100-GPUs und 40 Gigabyte Speicher geht es von 1,475 Dollar auf 1,696 Dollar. Beide Veränderungen entsprechen ebenfalls einem Plus von rund 15 Prozent.

## Auch ältere A100-Chips sind von der Anpassung betroffen

Dass auch die A100-Generation einbezogen wird, ist bemerkenswert, weil Nvidia inzwischen deutlich leistungsfähigere Chipgenerationen wie H100, H200, B200 und B300 anbietet. AWS führt die A100 jedoch weiterhin für anspruchsvolle Machine-Learning-Anwendungen.

...

## On-Demand und Savings Plans bleiben unverändert

Die Preisanpassung betrifft ausdrücklich nicht sämtliche Möglichkeiten, GPU-Leistung über Amazon EC2 zu beziehen. AWS erklärt, dass andere EC2-Capacity-Block-Preise sowie Festpreismodelle wie On-Demand und Savings Plans unverändert bleiben.

Damit lässt sich die Änderung nicht als allgemeine Erhöhung der AWS GPU-Preise verstehen. Sie betrifft ein spezielles Reservierungsmodell, bei dem Kunden verfügbare Beschleunigerkapazität für einen bestimmten Zeitraum sichern. Der Preis wird bei der Buchung festgelegt und im Voraus berechnet. Nach Abschluss einer Reservierung verändert sich der vereinbarte Betrag nicht mehr.

AWS weist darauf hin, dass die Preise für Capacity Blocks von der verfügbaren Kapazität und der Nachfrage zum Zeitpunkt der Buchung abhängen. Kunden können dabei unter anderem Zeitraum, Dauer und Umfang der gewünschten Kapazität auswählen. Bereits seit Einführung des Modells werden diese Preise nicht als dauerhaft feste Tarife behandelt.

results.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP Cloud GPU Pricing [2026]
results.author: Sana Rahman
highlights:
Cloud GPU pricing used to be a simple spreadsheet exercise: look up the hourly rate for an H100 instance, multiply by the hours you need, pick the cheapest provider. In October 2026 that spreadsheet broke. AWS raised its Blackwell B200 Capacity Block rate by roughly 15% on October 7, Microsoft Azure is one of the only major clouds still publishing a flat per-GPU hourly rate for H100 capacity, and Google Cloud has yet to post an official list price for H100, H200 or B200 instances at all. Comparing AWS vs Azure vs GCP cloud GPU pricing now means comparing three different billing philosophies, not just three price tags.

...

The three major hyperscalers no longer sell GPU capacity the same way. AWS leans heavily on EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, a reservation product with dynamic pricing that changes with supply and demand rather than a fixed rate card. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks documentation confirms Capacity Blocks can reserve up to 64 instances, or as many as 512 H100 GPUs, with reservations bookable up to eight weeks in advance. That flexibility is useful for training runs with a known start date, but it also means there is no single “AWS H100 price” the way there used to be with plain on-demand EC2.

...

Google Cloud sits at the opposite end: its A3 (H100), A3 Ultra (H200) and A4 (B200) instance families are confirmed to exist and to use those specific Nvidia GPUs, but no official Google Cloud page in the current research set states a public hourly price for any of them.

...

What AWS has not done, at least not in any officially confirmed source available as of October 23, 2026, is publish a flat on-demand hourly price for P5, P5e, P5en or P6-B200. Capacity Block pricing is explicitly dynamic, and AWS’s public materials direct buyers to request a quote or check the Capacity Blocks console rather than read a rate card.

...

Azure’s current GPU VM lineup for AI training includes NC40ads H100 v5, ND96isr H100 v5 and ND96isr H200 v5. Two of those SKUs give us the cleanest published numbers in this entire comparison. The NC40ads H100 v5 size, a single-H100 configuration, carried a reported East US pay-as-you-go Linux rate of $6.98 per hour as of October 19, 2026. The larger ND96isr H100 v5 size, which packs eight H100 GPUs, was reported at $98.32 per VM-hour in East US on the same date, which works out to $12.29 per GPU-hour.

Azure also lists an ND96isr H200 v5 size with eight H200 GPUs carrying 141 GB of memory each, making it the newest Hopper-class GPU family Azure has confirmed. Microsoft has not published an officially confirmed Azure B200 virtual machine family or hourly price as of October 23, 2026. Separately, Microsoft Foundry’s managed-compute tier, still in preview, bills hourly per accelerator across A100, H1 ... , H200 and MI300 GPU families, but Microsoft’s documentation says rates vary by accelerator family, region, deployment scope and commitment term, and directs customers to the Azure Pricing Calculator rather than a published table.

...

## Cloud GPU Pricing Compared: What’s Published vs What’s a Black Box

This is the table that matters most for anyone trying to budget an AI training run, and it is deliberately conservative: it only includes rates that each provider has actually published, rather than third-party estimates.

| GPU | AWS (published rate) | Azure (published rate) | Google Cloud (published rate) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, single GPU | No flat rate published; Capacity Blocks price dynamically | $6.98/hour, NC40ads H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H100, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | $98.32/hour ($12.29/GPU-hour), ND96isr H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H200, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | No flat on-demand VM rate confirmed in official sources | Not published |
| B200, per GPU-hour (Capacity Block) | $14.208/hour, effective Oct. 7, 2026, up from $12.355/hour (about a 15% increase) | Not offered / not confirmed | Not published; A4 uses Flex-start scheduling instead of a flat rate |

Independent GPU-rental trackers fill in some of the gaps, but their numbers are estimates rather than official list prices and should be read that way. ... 2, 2 ... 2 ... H20 ... (A ... ) and B200 (A4), but the ... - ... price for those configurations, since they were marked as not available for direct ... , so ... Google ... one.

...

## The October 7 AWS B200 Price Hike, Explained

The single clearest pricing move any of the three providers made in the last three months was AWS’s. Effective October 7, 2026, AWS raised its P6-B200 Capacity Block price from $12.355 to $14.208 per accelerator-hour, an increase of approximately 15%, according to GPU-pricing trackers Axis Intelligence and Dev.to’s FastGPU column, which independently captured the same before-and-after figures. For an eight-GPU P6-B200 node, the current instance-hour rate is about $113.666, a noticeable jump in monthly spend for teams running sustained training jobs.

AWS frames Capacity Block pricing as dynamic by design, moving with supply and demand rather than sitting on a fixed card, so a mid-quarter increase is consistent with how the product is supposed to work. It is also a useful data point for the “which cloud is cheapest” question: it shows that even the provider with the most reservation flexibility, AWS, is not necessarily the cheapest or the most stable option for Blackwell-class capacity right now. Teams planning a long B200 training run in Q4 2026 should budget for the possibility of another adjustment before their reservation window closes, since trackers reported this was not the first GPU list-price increase AWS made in recent months.

results.title: AWS posts new Capacity Block GPU rates effective October 7. · Sayer
results.author: Sayer Staff
highlights:
Amazon Web Services has posted new reservation rates for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, effective October 7, 2026. The prices are hourly, per accelerator: $16.146 for P6-B300 ($16.819 in AWS GovCloud), $14.208 for P6-B200 ($14.801 in GovCloud), $7.895 for P5en, $6.866 for P5e, $5.970 for P5, $2.546 for P4de, and $1.696 for P4d. AWS did not state a percentage.

The company says Capacity Block prices move with supply and demand and are updated from time to time. On its pricing page it says the new rates apply across available regions for those families. It also says every other EC2 Capacity Block price stays the same, and that prices on fixed models such as On-Demand and Savings Plans do not change. UltraServer and Trainium Capacity Block rates are on the current tables and are not in the October 7 list.

A Capacity Block is charged at the rate in effect when the customer buys it, AWS says, even if the block is scheduled to start after a later update. The fee is paid up front.

...

AWS limits the posted change to the Capacity Block families listed, and it says other Capacity Block prices, On-Demand, and Savings Plans are unchanged. The current tables still show more than one regional rate for some families, including P5 and P5en, while the October 7 notice states a single rate for each of those names. AWS does not say every current regional row rises by the same share.

results.title: AWS just raised reserved GPU prices again. This is the fourth hike this year. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
AWS just raised reserved GPU prices again. This is the fourth hike this year.

Effective Oct 7, AWS Capacity Block rates climb to $5.97/hr for H100 (up from $5.19) and $16.15/hr for B300. That puts H100 and B300 on AWS up 40 to 75% since January.

Our marketplace rate for H100 is still $2.01/hr. For B300 it is $5.85/hr. Neither has moved all year.

Our H100 rate is 66% below AWS's new rate, and our B300 rate is 64% below AWS's new rate, for the same chip on the same day. Spheron is a marketplace, not a single cloud, so prices do not quietly creep up every quarter.

results.title: 15 GPU list prices rose in September and none fell. Today AWS raises Capacity Blocks 15% — WPS
highlights:
FastGPU compared 176 posted on-demand GPU prices across September 2026: 15 rose, 0 fell. From October 7, AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML cost 15% more per GPU-hour, up to 26.5% outside the US.

 Dev.to · 2026-10-07 

 

In September 2026 we compared 176 posted on-demand GPU prices, each cloud's own published rate for each GPU it rents, between the first three and the last three days of the month. 15 ended the month higher, none ended it lower, and the other 161 did not move.

Today, October 7, AWS adds an increase of its own to EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML.

Everything below comes from the daily prices FastGPU records across GPU clouds, published as an open dataset, and from AWS's own pricing page. Every figure links to the page it comes from.

...

All 15 came from two providers: Verda (10) and RunPod (5). Marketplaces, where each host sets its own price, are not part of this count.

...

## The cheapest offer moves both ways 

The floor, the lowest posted on-demand price outside the hyperscalers (geometric mean of the first three days against the last three), is set by one or two providers at a time, so it swings:

- H100 SXM: $1.34 to $1.57 (+17.4%, set by 2 providers)
- H200: $2.60 to $2.16 (-17.1%, set by 2 providers)
- B200: $3.69 to $3.69 (0.0%, set by 1 provider)
- A100 80GB: $0.64 to $0.53 (-16.7%, set by 1 provider)

So the list prices at the larger GPU clouds drifted up while the cheapest deal stayed a moving target. For a job of a few hours, the floor is what you pay; for a quarter's budget, the list-price trend matters more.

...

## AWS Capacity Blocks: 15% more from today, up to 26.5% outside the US 

AWS's Capacity Blocks pricing page says:

> Effective October 7, 2026, hourly rates per accelerator across all available AWS Regions will be: P6-B300 at $16.146 ($16.819 in AWS GovCloud Regions), P6-B200 at $14.208 ($14.801 in AWS GovCloud Regions), P5en at $7.895, P5e at $6.866, P5 at $5.970, P4de at $2.546, and P4d at $1.696.

Against the rates AWS published before, as recorded in our price-change log, per GPU per hour:

AWS now charges one rate in every Region, so blocks that used to be cheaper outside the US (P5 and P5en) rise the most. AWS publishes these rates to a tenth of a cent; our log shows them rounded to the cent. AWS also says Capacity Block reservation prices are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand, and: "All other EC2 Capacity Block prices, as well as prices on fixed pricing models like On-Demand and Savings Plans, remain unchanged."

## What it means if you rent 

- A Capacity Block is reserved capacity: you book a start date and a length, and AWS guarantees the GPUs for it. That is a different product from an on-demand GPU you can stop at any time. Still, for scale: the cheapest posted H100 SXM is $1.79/hr at Vast.ai as of 2026-10-07 01:46 UTC, the September-end median across 16 providers was $3.70/hr, and a P5 Capacity Block is now $5.970/hr.
- If you were planning a reserved block, re-run the numbers: the reserve-or-rent calculator has the October 7 rates, and the GPU cluster page prices N GPUs for M months across providers' published term rates.
- List prices change without notice. A price alert emails you when a GPU drops below a price you choose, with no account.

## Data and method 

Posted prices, not transactions. The September report is computed from the recorded daily prices once the month is over and then frozen; every dated change is in the price-change log, also as JSON at `https://fastgpu.co/api/v1/price-changes`. The daily series is an open dataset (CC BY 4.0). Live prices in this post are as of 2026-10-07 01:46 UTC; the linked pages show the current ones. Some provider links on FastGPU are affiliate links; tables and every "cheapest" figure are ordered strictly by price.

results.title: AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at
results.author: Paul Nugent
highlights:
AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at the same price.

This is the most important AI infrastructure pricing story of the year, and the signal is unmistakable.

The move: ~20% price increase on EC2 Capacity Block reservations for Nvidia GPU instances, effective July 1. AWS cited "supply and demand dynamics" — meaning the global compute crunch has gotten severe enough that AWS believes customers will pay more without leaving.

results.title: Cloud GPU Pricing 2026: H100, B200 and RTX Rental Costs
results.author: Boris Sedu
highlights:
- An H100 costs about $2–12 per GPU-hour on demand depending on the provider: around $2 on marketplaces, $4–6 on AI-focused clouds such as Lambda, RunPod, Nebius and CoreWeave, and $7–12 on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Oracle.
- Newer GPUs cost more per hour but not always per job. A B200 rents for about $6.70–8.50 on AI clouds, but it trains roughly twice as fast as an H100, so the total cost of a job can be the same or lower.
- Consumer and mid-range GPUs are cheap: an RTX 4090 or RTX 5090 rents for roughly $0.30–1.20 per hour, an A100 80GB for $0.70–3.50.
- Prices rose in 2026. Nebius raised on-demand prices by about 17–21% on October 1, AWS raised Capacity Block prices three times, and several clouds moved the H100 from $2.99 to $3.99 per hour.
- Newer GPUs and better software change the math. In MLPerf Training 2026, NVIDIA’s GB300 was 1.3–1.6 times faster than the GB200, and the independent ClusterMAX rating put CoreWeave and Nebius at the top for cluster quality.
- Spot and reserved capacity cut costs by roughly 30–80%, but spot instances can be interrupted at any moment, and reservations lock you in.

...

For several years cloud ... Demand for AI compute kept growing, new Blackwell GPUs were scarce, and the global shortage of memory chips pushed up the cost of new servers.

- Nebius raised on-demand prices on October 1, 2026: H100 from $3.85 to $4.50 per hour, H200 from $4.50 to $5.40, B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.

- RunPod and Lambda list the H100 SXM at $3.99 per hour; in spring 2026 both were quoted at $2.99 or less. RunPod’s B200 rose from about $5.89 to $7.99.
